issues.legal_issue: A land-ceiling authority must notify an interested claimant and await the decision of a pending title suit disclosed to it before continuing the ceiling determination concerning the disputed land.
material_facts: The landholder’s return disclosed that a relative claimed part of the land and had filed a pending civil suit concerning title to it.
The authority proceeded with the ceiling determination without serving that claimant or awaiting the civil court’s decision.
The civil suit was later decreed in the claimant’s favour, leaving the landholder with no holding in excess of the ceiling limit.
issues.conclusion: The authority breached the statutory requirements by proceeding without notice to the interested claimant and without awaiting the decision in the pending title suit; the first appellate court correctly set aside the ceiling action.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 11(3) and 11(4) of the Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960 require service of the draft statement on all persons interested in the land and require the competent authority to await a competent court’s decision when the title question is already pending there. These requirements also give effect to natural justice. Article 300A of the Constitution requires deprivation of property to be in accordance with the procedure established by law.

predicates.agricultural_land_ceiling_proceeding: An authority is determining whether agricultural land held by a person exceeds a prescribed ceiling.
predicates.pending_title_suit_disclosed_to_authorit: A party informs the authority that a civil suit concerning title to some of the land is pending.
predicates.title_suit_unresolved: The civil court has not yet decided the title dispute when the authority is considering the landholding.

issues.definition: When a land-ceiling proceeding involves a disclosed, unresolved title suit, the authority must notify the interested claimant and await the civil court’s decision.

issues.legal_issue: An express civil-suit remedy concerning a title determination made in a land-ceiling proceeding falls within the exception to a general bar on civil-court jurisdiction.
material_facts: The landholder brought a civil suit challenging the action taken to acquire land as surplus.
The State argued that the civil court lacked jurisdiction and that the landholder should have used the statutory appeal or revision process.
The Court relied on the statutory provision permitting a civil suit to set aside a competent authority’s title order and on its earlier decision recognizing that remedy.
issues.conclusion: The general bar on civil-court jurisdiction does not exclude a civil suit where the governing law expressly permits one; the Court restored the first appellate court’s judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 46 of the Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960 begins with an exception for matters expressly provided for in that Act. Section 11(5) permits a party to sue in the civil court to set aside an order made by the competent authority under Section 11(4), and makes the civil court’s decision binding on that authority. Competent Authority, Tarana District, Ujjain (M.P.) v. Vijay Gupta & Ors., 1991 Supp (2) SCC 631, recognizes this remedy. The Court also considered State of Madhya Pradesh & Anr. v. Dungaji (Dead) Represented by Legal Representatives & Anr., (2019) 7 SCC 465, concerning the Act’s appeal and revision scheme, but held that the statutory scheme had been breached on the facts.

predicates.civil_suit_proceeding: A party brings a civil-court suit concerning a determination made in a land-ceiling proceeding.
predicates.express_civil_suit_remedy_available: The governing law expressly permits a party to bring a civil suit to challenge the relevant authority’s title determination.

issues.definition: When a civil suit concerns a determination for which the governing law expressly allows suit, the general jurisdictional bar does not exclude the civil court.

issues.legal_issue: A court may infer that missing official records would support a party’s account when the responsible authority fails to produce those records after being directed to do so and warned of the consequence.
material_facts: The Court directed the State to produce the records containing the landholder’s objections and gave further time to comply.
The Court warned that failure to produce the records would result in an adverse inference.
The State did not produce the records and later stated that they could not be traced.
The State’s own pleadings acknowledged that the landholder’s return referred to the pending title suit.
issues.conclusion: The Court inferred that the landholder had properly disclosed the pending suit in the return.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the failure to produce records after a production direction and an express warning as warranting an adverse inference. No separate statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this inference.

predicates.appellate_review_of_land_ceiling_action: A court is reviewing an appeal concerning action taken in a land-ceiling proceeding.
predicates.court_ordered_record_production: The court directed the responsible authority to produce records relevant to a disputed factual issue.
predicates.responsible_authority_failed_to_produce_: The authority did not produce the ordered records despite being warned that nonproduction could have an evidentiary consequence.

issues.definition: In an appellate review of land-ceiling action, failure by the responsible authority to produce ordered records after warning permits the court to infer that the pending title suit was disclosed.
